title: Why Sunrun Stock Surged 33.4% This Week
detail:
Why Sunrun Stock Surged 33.4% This Week
Scott Levine, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 1:17 PM CST 4 min read
RUN
^GSPC
Trade Sunrun on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A third-quarter earnings report featuring $1.1 billion in revenue sent Sunrun (NASDAQ:RUN) soaring 33.4% this week.

Sunrun stock changed hands at $9.98 as of the close on Friday, Nov. 6, up 33.4% from Friday, Oct. 30's close, according to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence. Across those five sessions, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 2.7%, and the Nasdaq-100 fell 4.9%.

Image source: Getty Images.

Third-quarter revenue beat overshadows trimmed guidance

On Wednesday, Sunrun reported third-quarter revenue of $1.1 billion, a 51.7% year-over-year jump that topped Wall Street estimates. Diluted earnings per share reached $0.56, beating the consensus expectation of $0.32 per share. That top-line surge came even as installed solar capacity dropped 15% year over year, because Sunrun completed a strategic shift toward direct-channel volume while scaling higher-margin battery storage attachments.

Sunrun sells and leases residential solar panels and home battery systems to homeowners seeking lower electricity bills and backup power. The company makes money through upfront installations and multi-year subscription agreements. That recurring service model generates steady subscriber value, but it requires heavy debt financing to build systems before collecting monthly customer payments.

Management trimmed its full-year cash generation outlook to roughly $200 million, the bottom of its previous $200 million to $375 million target range. Even with that reduced guidance, direct sales volume grew 9% year over year as battery attachment rates hit a record 75%. This week's quarterly beat proves Sunrun can expand system margins through battery storage, but trimming guidance to the bottom of its range keeps cash generation on a tight leash.

High debt loads and policy shifts remain key risks

Even after this week's rally, Sunrun remains down 55% from its 52-week high of $21.95, reflecting long-term investor anxiety over rising interest rates and complex project financing.

Sunrun trades at a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 5, though that low multiple is heavily influenced by non-cash accounting adjustments and derivative gains. The company carried $15.3 billion in total debt, including lease obligations, as of Sept. 30, 2026, against $699.4 million in cash and short-term investments as of Sept. 30, 2026. Investors will watch the next quarterly earnings report scheduled for Feb. 25, 2027, to see if direct installation growth can offset higher funding costs.

With the S&P 500 currently yielding around 1.1%, income-focused investors may want to consider high-quality dividend stocks offering higher yields. Lowe's Companies (NYSE: LOW) is such an example. With a forward dividend yield of around 2.3%, it yields more than twice that of this major market index.

That's not all. It's also one of the Dividend Kings, or stocks with more than 50 years of consecutive dividend growth. For 55 consecutive years, the home improvement retailer has raised its payout.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Although continued sluggishness in the housing market remains a major issue for the company, at current prices, this may be one of the best blue chip dividend stocks to buy today.

Image source: Getty Images.
Lowe's and its dividend bona fides

Last May, Lowe's implemented its latest dividend hike, increasing its quarterly payout 4%, from $1.20 to $1.25 per share. Admittedly, this represents a slowdown in dividend growth. Over the past three years, annual payout growth has averaged 6.4%, while over the last five years, it has averaged 15.6%.

This is largely due to the aforementioned housing-market-related headwind, which has, in turn, affected the company's growth. Earnings have declined in recent years, with diluted EPS of $13.20 for the fiscal year ended January 2024, $12.23 for the fiscal year ended January 2025, and $11.85 for the fiscal year ended January 2026.

However, after this extended slump, better results may be just around the corner. Per analyst estimates, Lowe's earnings could come in at $12.30 per share this fiscal year, and at nearly $13 for the fiscal year ending January 2028. Moreover, because Lowe's has slowed the pace of its dividend increases, the company now has a fairly low payout ratio, the percentage of earnings allocated to dividends.

Lowe's forward payout ratio is around 41%. For comparison, Lowe's largest competitor, Home Depot, has a forward payout ratio of 65%, meaning less margin for error.

Stay for the rebound

Alongside a sustainable, growing dividend, Lowe's has other strengths in its corner. The company continues its pivot toward the professional segment of the construction space through acquisitions such as last year's purchase of Foundation Building Materials. Besides having a lower payout ratio than rival Home Depot, it also trades at a lower valuation, 16 times forward earnings, versus 21 times forward earnings for Lowe's larger competitor.

PepsiCo: $71 in income

title: Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue
detail:
Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue

Every member of Wall Street's "Magnificent Seven" now wants its stock kept off OKX and ICE's planned tokenized stock venue.

Apple and Meta Platforms are among 11 companies added to the list of objecting issuers in an updated notice from OKXICE TSV dated Thursday.

They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia and Tesla, completing a sweep by the group of tech giants that makes up a large share of the S&P 500's value. The other new objectors are Home Depot, Boeing, GE Vernova, Palantir, ServiceNow, S&P Global, KLA, Super Micro Computer and Nebius Group, bringing the total number of companies saying "no" to the OKX and ICE platform to 67.

Meta's objection carries some irony. The Facebook parent once tried to launch its own stablecoin, Libra, later renamed Diem, before abandoning the project in 2022 amid regulatory pushback.

Apple had been one of the last megacaps missing from the list after Amazon, Tesla, and SpaceX objected in the venue's Nov. 2 notice. The tally stood at 56 then, and at nine on Oct. 15, when the first objectors appeared.

Just as notable is who hasn't objected. Crypto-friendly public companies such as Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy don't appear on the list. Coinbase launched tokenized stocks for non-U.S. users on its Base network in August. Berkshire Hathaway, Visa, and Exxon Mobil are also absent. It's unclear whether OKXICE notified those companies.

Under the SEC's innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can't make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC's order. It's worth noting, though, that the objection applies only to that venue.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX's U.S. holding company, plans to offer tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain. An outside "tokenizer" would hold real shares one-for-one through a registered broker-dealer.

With the market's biggest names opted out, it's unclear which major stocks the venue will be able to offer at launch, and its notices don't list the tokens it plans to make available.

Keith Noonan, The Motley Fool

At the start of this year, Warren Buffett stepped down as Berkshire Hathaway's (NYSE: BRKA)(NYSE: BRKB) CEO and passed the reins to current CEO Greg Abel. Then, in September, Buffett stepped down as the chairman of the company's board of directors.

Sometimes called "the Oracle of Omaha" in reference to his birthplace and incredible history of investment success, the famously successful, 96-year-old moneyman is winding down his active participation with Berkshire. He's had a legendary run. Over roughly six decades, the Buffett-led investment conglomerate managed to post an average annualized return of roughly 19% -- nearly doubling the S&P 500's average annual return rate of roughly 10% across the stretch.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

To put things in perspective, if you had invested $5,000 in Berkshire and held it over a 60-year period, that investment would now be worth roughly $170.5 million. Meanwhile, the same buy-and-hold strategy with the S&P 500 would have grown your position to roughly $1.5 million across the same stretch. With that incredible performance difference in mind, can investors still rely on Buffett's playbook to deliver incredible, market-crushing returns?

Buffett's core philosophies remain invaluable, but don't ignore modern context

The importance of identifying strong businesses that are worth holding for the long term has been central to Buffett and Berkshire's incredible wins through the decades. Buffett believed that the stock market was an engine for transferring wealth from the impatient and overly active to those who were patient and had a long-term view and conviction in the strengths of their strategies. With regard to how that approach panned out for him, the proof is in the pudding.

Buffett's focus on backing strong businesses that traded at non-prohibitive valuations was central to Berkshire's success over more than six decades. As a student of value investing pioneer Benjamin Graham, Warren Buffett used valuation tools -- including discounted free cash flow analysis and return on equity -- to identify investment opportunities with risk-reward profiles that tilted dynamics in his company's favor.

On the other hand, Buffett's frame also foregrounded the importance of being willing to pay what looked like a valuation premium when a company's strengths could justify it. One of his most famous investing adages is that "it's better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than to buy a fair company at a wonderful price." With a great company, that "fair price" has the potential to turn into wonderful value over time as the strengths of the business produce compounding results. This philosophy extended to both Berkshire's investments in publicly traded stocks and businesses that it acquired outright.

Daniel Foelber, The Motley Fool

The major stock market indexes rallied following midterm election results, with the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) up 1.6% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES: ^DJI) gaining 3% on the session. From a sector perspective, the biggest winners were healthcare and consumer staples -- both of which closed at all-time highs. Amid Republican control of the Executive Branch and Democrats gaining the majority in the Senate and House, investors are piling into safe sectors that tend to do well regardless of political and economic uncertainty.

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (NYSEMKT: SCHD) -- which we'll simply refer to as SCHD going forward -- is heavily concentrated in these sectors. So it's no surprise it added to its already red-hot gains to close at an all-time high. Meanwhile, McDonald's (NYSE: MCD) roared 6.5% higher on Nov. 4 but is still down big year-to-date. Here's why McDonald's stands out as an even better buy than SCHD.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
High income, high turnover

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which is rebalanced quarterly into a basket of high-yield dividend stocks. The rebalancing emphasizes yield. So the index will sometimes cycle out of stocks whose yields are declining because their stock prices are rising faster than their dividend growth rates. And similarly, it will cycle into stocks and sectors with rising yields.

In March, the ETF had a 23.9% energy sector weighting. But after multiple rebalances, the energy sector weighting fell to 15.4% as of Sept. 30. In market-cap-weighted indexes like the S&P 500, outperforming sectors gain higher weightings, not lower ones.

With less energy sector weighting, SCHD cycled into more consumer staples, healthcare, and high-yield technology stocks. The strategy is paying off, as the energy sector sold off while consumer staples and healthcare rose following the midterm election results. But this practice leads to heavy trading, with the ETF featuring a 40.6% portfolio turnover rate as of Sept. 30, 2026, which is unappealing to long-term investors looking to build a portfolio around core holdings.

All told, SCHD is a good ETF for generating passive income because it prioritizes allocating toward high-yield, industry-leading companies. But investors should be aware that its year-to-date gains are particularly high because SCHD has been rotating into hot sectors and out of cold sectors simply by the nature of its rules-based methodology -- not some magic formula. These mechanics are coincidentally maximizing gains this year. But that same method can backfire if a leading sector continues producing strong gains, or if a beaten-down sector continues to sell-off.
